(Este artigo contém muitos spoilers; leia com precaução)

Ontem, a versão 2.7 do «Mingchao», intitulada «O Amanhecer das Correntes Ocultas», foi lançada oficialmente.

Desde que foi divulgada, no final de setembro, as autoridades têm vindo a criar em torno desta versão uma sensação de «tempestade iminente» mais intensa do que nunca.

Seja o céu envolto em nuvens negras sobre a Torre de Li Na Xi no vídeo de antevisão, o misterioso caçador de demónios de cabelo branco, ou as informações fragmentadas que vêm sendo preparadas há muito tempo — como a «morte da Santa Donzela» — que surgem alternadamente, ou ainda a contagem decrescente para o lançamento da versão iniciada oficialmente nas principais plataformas sociais durante o feriado do Dia da República, todas estas ações estão a transmitir um sinal claro ao mundo exterior:«Mingchao» está prestes a atingir o clímax desta fase.

De um modo geral, as atualizações no final de uma grande versão de um jogo do mundo 2D desempenham frequentemente duas funções essenciais: em primeiro lugar, a síntese do conteúdo do ciclo atual, incluindo a resolução de pistas anteriores e o aperfeiçoamento da narrativa; em segundo lugar, servir de ponte entre o passado e o futuro, afinal, o fim de uma fase também significa o início de um novo capítulo.

É precisamente por isso que a importância da versão 2.7 é evidente.

Olhando para toda a fase 2.X, «Mingchao» trouxe aos jogadores inúmeras surpresas: as intrigas familiares e os conflitos de fé que se desenrolaram em Laguna, as lutas de gladiadores repletas de entusiasmo nas Sete Colinas e as sombras da «Maré Negra», onde correm águas subterrâneas, foram todas profundamente marcantes,Agora, a versão 2.7 não só vai encerrar a aventura dos jogadores na Torre de Linaxi, como também vai dar início a uma nova jornada.

Além disso, do ponto de vista do desenvolvimento do produto, a série 2.X representa um período crucial para o «Mingchao» na construção da sua competitividade central — «uma narrativa cinematográfica a serviço da construção das personagens» — e constitui, acima de tudo, a pedra angular para que o jogo enverede verdadeiramente por um caminho de operação sustentável a longo prazo.Muitas das experiências narrativas e tecnológicas cujo sucesso já foi comprovado necessitam, igualmente, de um clímax faseado adequado para as concluir.

Por isso, antes de se levantar o pano final, a expectativa da comunidade de jogadores não para de aumentar e a atmosfera em torno do desfecho vai-se intensificando cada vez mais.

Então, será que «Mingchao», que vem sendo desenvolvido até à versão 2.7, conseguirá corresponder a todas estas expectativas?

01

O Prólogo do Último Acto

Para responder a esta questão, convém, antes de mais, analisarmos que tipo de final *Mingchao* reservou para Li Na Xita.

Este último ato desenrolou-se lentamente sob o céu de Laguna, repleto de nuvens sombrias e chuva intensa, como se o destino estivesse a anunciar que o ponto de partida da viagem era também o seu fim.

Tal como quando chegaram pela primeira vez a Lagú, o sussurro de Christopher ressoou nos seus ouvidos, e os errantes mergulharam assim num sonho confuso que parecia prenunciar uma «tragédia»:Ao longo da estrada, viam-se figuras familiares que nos acompanharam na nossa viagem pela Torre de Linaxi, só que cada uma delas parecia estar aprisionada,Coletta estava sentada no chão, exausta; Juno parecia ainda não ter saído do casulo tecido pelo conhecimento; e Phoebe estava mergulhada numa oração silenciosa…

E, no fim do caminho, encontrava-se uma visão aterradora que parecia os restos mortais de Katishia.

Na ilusão, Katishia apresentava um rosto sem vida, com uma flor sinistra a desabrochar no peito. A pergunta de Christopher — «Quem domina o destino?» — despertou facilmente a memória dos jogadores; já às 2h30, tinha ficado claro que Katishia era o centro da conspiração.

Por outro lado, o caçador de demónios desconhecido, envolto em chamas cinzentas, lançou ao Santuário palavras frias e mortíferas.

Em seguida, enquanto os jogadores ainda não tinham recuperado a compostura, «Mingchao» acelerou rapidamente o enredo, lançando-lhes na cara a reviravolta impactante que foi a «morte da Santa Virgem». Imediatamente a seguir, apontou a irracionalidade do «assassinato», e a chave para desvendar o mistério voltou a recair sobre o misterioso caçador de demónios.

No momento em que a versão 2.7 mal tinha começado a revelar a história, *Mingchao* construiu uma cadeia narrativa densa através de cortes de câmara, de uma interpretação silenciosa na disposição dos cenários e de diálogos repletos de informação,Tudo o que os jogadores vêem complementa a narrativa e, de forma ainda mais engenhosa, ao criar um enredo cheio de reviravoltas, o jogo pré-estabelece na mente dos jogadores uma posição ambígua quanto ao caráter dos personagens UP, tornando difícil distinguir o bem do mal.

Nem sequer se esqueceram de incluir interlúdios humorísticos, ao estilo da banda «The Fool», para regular o ambiente.

No que diz respeito ao controlo do enredo, a atual versão de «Mingchao» já demonstra bastante destreza, um resultado alcançado através de pequenos avanços diários desde o início da versão 2.0.

Em seguida, a história avança: enquanto perseguia o rasto da Maré Negra, o Viajante reencontra Avidia e, ao lidar com a Maré Negra no Cofre de Motari juntamente com Coleta Zanni, depara-se com o falso Finlec criado pela Maré Negra.

A presença de alguém que não deveria estar ali, acompanhado pela Maré Negra, e a fusão entre a realidade e a fantasia são sinais precursores de que a Maré Negra está prestes a transbordar. A Maré Negra utiliza o poder do Leviatã para corromper as almas. O Errante descobre que a Caçadora de Demónios se chama Gabriella e, ao entrar na Caixa da Civilização, fica a conhecer a história de Lina Xita e o nascimento do Leviatã.

Esta narrativa completa a tónica central de toda a série 2.X, ou seja, «quem escreve a história». Será que o nascimento e a sobrevivência da civilização necessitam da orientação de uma entidade superior? Esta é a dúvida do Senhor dos Anos, Ying Bailadu, e talvez seja também uma alusão às reflexões que o Errante teve antes de perder a memória. E, evidentemente,ambos acreditam que a própria humanidade é a criadora da história e a cronista da época, e que só com as próprias forças a humanidade poderá alcançar um futuro que nem os Errantes, nem mesmo o Senhor do Ano, conseguem alcançar.

Já Avidia, esta personagem inventada por Christopher, no final da sua vida, irrompeu com uma chama de vontade que transcendeu a ficção, transformando-se num grito de vida de uma autenticidade incomparável.Esta personagem reflete o brilho da humanidade, segundo o qual, desde que se encerre a vontade de se tornar algo verdadeiro, o falso pode revelar-se mais real do que o verdadeiro.

Na minha opinião, o desfecho de Avidia volta, mais uma vez, a colocar em destaque o tema central de toda a narrativa da versão 2.x, ou seja, «ultrapassar o destino».

Ao rever toda a série 2.X, perceber-se-á que o palco da Torre de Li Na Xi está repleto de lutas e rebeliões da vontade individual obstinada perante o peso do destino — tal como Juno face à profecia, Mi Ya face ao título de campeã e Coleta face à família, entre muitos outros exemplos,cada personagem, quer seja protagonista ou NPC, lança um ataque humano contra o moinho do destino.

O décimo ato do segundo capítulo de «Mingchao», ou seja, esta secção, o prólogo do ato final,chegou ao ponto em que foram resolvidas todas as pistas que se arrastaram ao longo de várias versões. Este prólogo do ato final revela a resposta definitiva desta aventura — ou seja, a reflexão sobre a civilização — e, ao mesmo tempo, condensa a essência narrativa de toda a versão 2.x, continuando a escrever o núcleo espiritual da Torre de Li Na Xi.

O Décimo Act tem como espinha dorsal uma grande quantidade de texto; a integração harmoniosa entre imagens CG pré-renderizadas, imagens CG geradas em tempo real, gravuras interativas e sequências QTE constitui a sua essência. O resultado final é a concretização de todo o sólido trabalho narrativo acumulado por «Mingchao» ao longo do último ano.

02

O final de espetáculo em que todos dançam

Como construir um clímax narrativo digno de uma «batalha final»? A resposta dada por *Mingchao* é: no meio de um rio de desespero, reunir a luz da esperança através da união de todas as pessoas.

Quando os errantes acompanharam Gabriella até às Sete Colinas, a maré negra alastrou-se, os guerreiros reuniram-se e percorreram o Paraíso para disfarçar a essência da destruição com esplendor.O cavaleiro do Oriente, «Qiu Yuan», trouxe a expiação do bispo Finleck; entre as fendas do desespero, a esperança ainda perdura; a batalha final está iminente, e o clima está tenso e cheio de apreensão.

Em momentos de perigo, apesar de os gladiadores de Qichou serem destemidos e não temerem a morte, a desvantagem natural em termos de número acabou por se revelar o seu ponto fraco mais fatal. Quando a Maré Negra estava prestes a abater-se sobre eles, um coluna de luz azul que se ergueu no ar trouxe a todos a ajuda de Laguna e até da Costa Negra.

Graças ao apoio de todos, o errante pôde seguir os passos de Gabriella sem preocupações, dando início à «viagem descendente» que o levaria a percorrer o Paraíso.

Esta viagem não foi nada fácil; a maldade fluía por todo o lado. O barqueiro do rio Estige, que era o líder da Sociedade da Estrela Murcha, impediu Gabriella — a única ajuda do Errante no Inferno — de avançar, enquanto Christopher, mais uma vez, arrastou o Errante para uma ilusão ainda mais cruel.

Por outro lado, no solo, o ataque conjunto de Florlo, o Marcado, destruiu a frágil linha de defesa, que já se encontrava à beira do colapso; os combatentes, que ainda não tinham tomado o elixir capaz de resistir à erosão da Maré Negra, foram engolidos pela Maré Negra que se abateu sobre eles.

O errante que caiu na escuridão chegou a um lugar de vazio, onde se revela um futuro ainda mais cru e despojado. Cada personagem que tanto aprecias ergueu um túmulo ilusório.

O nome gravado naquela lápide, tal como a ironia de Christopher, parecia transformar-se num prego de aço que se cravava no teu peito.

Este cemitério, símbolo da destruição, parece anunciar um desfecho trágico, inevitável e com um significado incontestável na realidade.

Mas será mesmo assim?

Hegel, na sua obra «Estética», estabeleceu claramente a distinção entre a comédia e a tragédia. Na sua opinião, a chamada comédia é aquela em que «a subjetividade prevalece», o que pode ser simplesmente entendido como os personagens da peça dominarem o enredo; tal como no caso do «Mingchao», em que o errante, desde que aja com determinação, consegue salvar Yuno,derrotar o falso rei, entre outras coisas.

Já na tragédia acontece o contrário: muitas vezes, as personagens ficam presas aos limites impostos pelo chamado destino e, por mais que exerçam a sua autonomia, seja através de ações concretas ou não, não conseguem romper as amarras que lhes foram impostas, tal como acontece em «Hamlet», onde o destino inelutável da morte paira sobre a figura de Hamlet.

De acordo com a narrativa das versões do «Mingchao» desde a 2.X, com exceção das partes relacionadas com Floro, penso que tudo o resto pode ser enquadrado na categoria da comédia de Hegel.

E, tal como demonstrado no décimo ato, mantendo o cerne inalterado desde o início, a versão 2.7 não é, evidentemente, uma exceção.No entanto, «Mingchao», com a sua capacidade de mobilizar emoções cada vez mais aperfeiçoada e com o volume narrativo de dois capítulos inteiros, explora ao máximo o potencial do conflito dramático, conferindo a esta comédia um tom narrativo repleto de reviravoltas.

Gabriella, na sua luta contra o destino, acendeu a chama do ódio que, neste momento, é a chama da esperança que rompe o desespero.

Ela derrotou a encarnação do presidente da Sociedade das Estrelas Rescalonadas e apresentou-se perante o Errante, revelando-te, ao mesmo tempo, que o que vês diante de ti não passa de uma projeção da tua mente, sob a influência da Maré Negra. E este lugar não é, de forma alguma, o fim da viagem do Errante, mas sim o seu ponto de partida.

A aurora boreal rasga a longa noite e, nas palavras de Gabriella, um caminho formado pela união de pequenos pontos de luz substitui o cemitério em ruínas por onde os errantes passaram. Acompanhando os teus passos, a cada momento a luz das estrelas eleva-se, e com ela, uma voz calorosa que te é tão familiar chega aos teus ouvidos.

Sabes, esses feixes de luz que te guiam e dissipam o desespero são os teus antigos companheiros, o povo da Torre de Li Na Xi. A sua vontade, impulsionada pela essência da Maré Negra — «o desejo de ligação» —, invadiu o mar da tua alma, ultrapassou as barreiras do teu coração e entrou em ressonância contigo.

Superando os obstáculos criados pela «Associação das Estrelas Resquícios», formada pelos demónios da mente, a verdadeira batalha final dá-se início.

E mesmo que se obtivesse o poder de Ingbailado, depois de a «Espada dos Direitos Humanos» ter conseguido separar Katixia, perante a torrente imparável formada pelo Esqueleto Sonoro de Lina Xita, pelos Sintonizadores e por todos os caminhos percorridos, bem como por todas as vontades e forças dispersas reunidas, qualquer lamento cessaria.

Já nem preciso dizer o quão fluido é o CG pré-renderizado no final.

Após a descarga emocional da batalha final, a sombra de Meiji dissipou-se,a Torre de Li Na Xi deu as boas-vindas à era em que «Deus está morto», Avidia tornou-se um verdadeiro herói, Finlek completou a sua redenção e realizou o desejo de longa data dos Soberanos das gerações passadas; mesmo que as ruínas deixadas pela catástrofe ainda precisem de ser reconstruídas e a Ordem das Estrelas Resquiciadas volte a adormecer nas trevas, neste momento,a história de Li Na Xita chegou, de facto, a um final feliz.

Quanto ao final do episódio 2.7, embora haja quem possa considerá-lo um cliché, numa obra de fantasia, sentir o alívio que advém de superar a crueldade e retirar daí a coragem para enfrentar a realidade é precisamente o significado imortal destes finais felizes.

Após a atualização de ontem, no NGA, alguns jogadores lançaram espontaneamente uma votação sobre o grau de satisfação com o desfecho da versão 2.7. Penso que este tópico, com mais de mil participantes, é a melhor resposta à questão colocada no início do artigo: se a versão 2.7 correspondeu às expectativas dos jogadores.

E o poema de despedida que paira no final da jornada — tecido a partir das sucessivas encontros do Viajante na Torre de Li Na Xi —, com a leve sensação de relutância que dele emana, talvez venha a tornar-se, no coração de cada jogador de «Ming Chao», uma «memória exclusiva» da Torre de Li Na Xi.

03

Conclusão: O caminho percorrido

Em tempos, Li Songlun, num período difícil logo após o início do teste público de «Mingchao», afirmou publicamente: «Conseguir sobreviver é, por si só, a perspetiva de longo prazo para o produto “Mingchao”».

Hoje em dia, o estado em que se encontra «Mingchao» ultrapassa claramente o âmbito que esta frase consegue resumir.

Embora seja difícil reproduzir palavra por palavra todo o enredo do capítulo «Li Na Xita», ao olhar para trás para toda a trajetória da versão 2.X de «Mingchao», verifica-se que, no que diz respeito à apresentação, o jogo abandonou praticamente os diálogos estáticos, optando por uma representação visual que combina a cinematografia com a interatividade do jogo para fazer avançar a história.

Por exemplo, na versão 2.7, na sequência em que a «Caixa da Civilização» revela a história da Torre de Li Na Xi, as gravuras interativas tornaram-se a principal forma de expressão; já nas imagens CG convencionais, surgiram indícios de opções temporárias. Embora estas últimas não tenham, por enquanto, a função de orientar o enredo para ramificações, proporcionam, sem dúvida, ao «Mingchao» possibilidades potenciais de uma narrativa em rede.

Além disso, num momento crucial do desenrolar da história, na versão 2.7, o ecrã de carregamento tradicional foi substituído pelo crescimento do «Coco da Maré Negra», utilizando fragmentos de informação ou imagens simbólicas que se enquadram na narrativa, de modo a que o próprio processo de espera se tornasse parte integrante da narrativa.

Merecem especial destaque os designs «Meta» que integram profundamente os mecanismos com a narrativa — por exemplo, a apresentação do espaço subconsciente do protagonista diretamente como a «página de início de sessão do jogo», fazendo com que cada início de sessão se torne um reflexo das imagens mentais da personagem, esbatendo assim a fronteira entre a jogabilidade e o enredo.

Além disso, depois de Gabriella ter derrotado o presidente da Sociedade das Estrelas Resquícios,o enredo avança, introduzindo uma perspetiva em primeira pessoa semelhante à de «Ghost Walker», bem como uma mecânica de jogo com alternância temporal semelhante à de «Titanfall 2», o que representa também uma iteração do «deslocamento simples» em primeira pessoa de Floro ou do Errante, presente na versão 2.0 inicial de «Mingchao».

Não é preciso dizer muito sobre o que constitui o cerne da expressividade da perspetiva na primeira pessoa: reside na construção de uma forte imersão narrativa através da perspetiva subjetiva, em que o jogador deixa de ser um mero observador para passar a «incorporar-se» diretamente no espaço visual e de ação de Gabriella. Este design torna ainda mais intenso o estilo de combate de Gabriella, inspirado na série «Devil May Cry».

Através desta cena, «Mingchao» transmite aos jogadores, de forma harmoniosa, os movimentos de Gabriella — que são claramente uma referência às «Duas Pistolas de Dante» — e as suas características de personalidade, enquanto o desempenho das armas já apresenta, de forma preliminar, uma linha de mira e feedback visual do recuo.

Pelo que sei, os obstáculos técnicos para concretizar esta experiência não são insignificantes, estando longe de se tratar de algo que se consiga simplesmente ajustando a posição da câmara.Em primeiro lugar, é necessária uma coordenação entre o movimento da personagem e a oscilação da câmara, para simular os micromovimentos reais da cabeça. Ao mesmo tempo, para evitar distorções na perspetiva em primeira pessoa, o «Mingchao» tem de calcular rigorosamente o ângulo de campo de visão e os parâmetros de desfoque dinâmico, evitando assim, desde a base, a vertigem de simulador que os jogadores possam sentir.

Em segundo lugar, trata-se de saber como, numa perspetiva na primeira pessoa, apresentar de forma engenhosa as expressões faciais e a interpretação corporal a que as cenas de transição tradicionais na terceira pessoa recorrem; isto requer, normalmente, o uso de animações programadas e da composição das imagens para orientar a atenção do jogador, garantindo que, mesmo com uma perspetiva limitada, as interpretações emocionais essenciais não passem despercebidas.

A este respeito, a solução provisória atual de «Mingchao» consiste numa combinação bastante direta de diálogos e acções, mas, na essência, este design não só constitui um teste de resistência à lógica do mecanismo de estados de animação e à capacidade de cálculo em tempo real do próprio «Mingchao», como também reflete a sua intenção de se alinhar com os elevados padrões da indústria no que diz respeito à integração entre a jogabilidade e a profundidade narrativa.Afinal, quem poderia imaginar que a inserção da perspetiva na primeira pessoa, no início da versão 2.0, evoluiria na versão 2.7 para uma componente concreta, responsável por inovações na jogabilidade e com funções narrativas?

Pode dizer-se que, da versão 2.0 à 2.7, o design de espetáculos de «Mingchao» passou por uma transformação qualitativa, evoluindo de uma acumulação de elementos visuais para uma integração da experiência.Na fase inicial da versão 2.0, o foco estava no aumento da densidade da apresentação; na fase intermédia, começaram a ser introduzidas interações QTE e interações com o cenário; e, na versão 2.7, todos os elementos — desde os ecrãs de carregamento e sequências CG até às mecânicas de jogo — foram integrados na dimensão da apresentação, criando um sistema de expressão completo e unificado.

É assim que funciona a revista «Mingchao»: semear, cultivar, florescer e dar frutos. De certa forma, talvez seja esta a razão fundamental pela qual consegue crescer contra a tendência do ciclo.

A versão 2.7 traz simultaneamente os capítulos 10 e 11 da história principal, permitindo aos jogadores vivenciar de uma só vez todo o clímax da narrativa. O regresso de Florolo e as inúmeras referências ocultas constituem não só uma forma de retribuir aos jogadores mais dedicados, como também refletem a perspicácia da equipa de produção em responder aos comentários da comunidade.

Além disso, as otimizações do sistema, tais como a redução da carga de desenvolvimento e a integração dos acessos às atividades, resultam diretamente das sugestões de longa data da comunidade de jogadores. É precisamente isto que o «Mingchao» tem vindo a fazer desde sempre.

Ao analisar a trajetória de desenvolvimento de «Mingchao» 2.0 do ponto de vista do produto, não é difícil perceber que a maturidade do sistema e os avanços nas apresentações demonstrados na versão 2.7 assentam, na essência, na escuta e na resposta contínuas à «experiência do jogador».

Para os jogadores, a versão 2.7 assemelha-se mais a uma resposta perfeita ao tema «laços» — com um final épico e grandioso e um retrato coletivo completo em que «todos estão de volta aos seus lugares», respondeu solenemente às expectativas e ao entusiasmo dos jogadores ao longo do último ano.

Já para o setor, a versão 2.7 de «Mingchao» marca mais um salto qualitativo da Kuro na capacidade de gestão do projeto. Da versão 2.0 à 2.7, a sua produtividade em termos de conteúdo não se diluiu devido às iterações frequentes; pelo contrário, cada grande versão gerou pontos de viragem que redefiniram a experiência de jogo.O que o jogo demonstra já não é um avanço tecnológico pontual, mas sim um sistema de conteúdos industrializado — iterável e reutilizável — que articula com precisão a narrativa, o conteúdo de alta densidade, a inovação na jogabilidade e a operação estável.

Esta capacidade de produzir conteúdos de alta qualidade, previsível e sustentável, poderá ser precisamente a chave para que a «Mingchao» construa a sua própria vantagem competitiva no meio da futura concorrência acirrada no setor dos conteúdos e no mercado saturado do mundo anime.

A despedida serve para um novo reencontro. A versão 2.7 também deixou mais pistas sobre a história futura: o verdadeiro nome de Abu, revelado pelo Leviatã; a possibilidade de utilizar o poder do Meio; e, conforme referido pelo presidente da Sociedade das Estrelas Resquiciosas, o local do terceiro caso e o palco do futuro, «La Helo»,Tudo isto serve como prenúncio de um mundo ainda mais vasto.

Indícios do período 1.1

O carnaval da Torre de Li Na Xi já chegou ao fim, e o novo capítulo de «Ming Chao» toma isto como ponto de partida, dando início, discretamente, a um cenário ainda mais grandioso.

title: Can a one-time purchase model really lead to effective growth for “evergreen games” designed for long-term operation?
text:
In today's gaming industry, it's becoming increasingly difficult to achieve overnight success.
Recently, Ma Xiaoyi, Senior Vice President of Tencent, mentioned in an interview that creating a long-lasting GaaS product might require “taking it one chapter at a time”—with long-term operation as the ultimate goal, the team might be able to gradually build and validate its capabilities in gameplay, storytelling, and other areas by developing single-player, one-time-purchase titles.
In terms of business models, service-based games offer far greater revenue sustainability and potential than single-player buy-to-play titles. But just as a carp leaps through the Dragon Gate, behind every successful, long-running game there may be countless competitors that have fallen by the wayside—and no one dares to claim with absolute certainty that they have mastered all the necessary conditions for success.Even Ma Xiaoyi admits that a game may need to meet 10 prerequisites just to qualify for the “lottery,” and even then, the odds of winning may be as low as 30 percent.
Developing evergreen games is challenging. If you have to consider long-term operations while refining gameplay and storytelling, the complexity increases exponentially. That’s why Tencent is open to breaking this process down internally and iterating over several generations, and it also supports teams exploring new approaches through single-player, one-time-purchase games.
This process is undoubtedly challenging: Developing a single-player game is relatively straightforward, but long-term operation, monetization, multiplayer online gameplay, social competition, cross-platform support… every keyword associated with creating a long-lasting game seems like an insurmountable barrier. Can the gap between buy-to-play and subscription-based games truly be bridged through accumulated experience?
In this episode of “Game & Tea Roundtable,” we spoke with industry professionals about whether developing single-player, buy-out games can truly contribute to the long-term growth of “evergreen games” designed for sustained operation.
▍Industry Troll: Xiao Jiu
It can, but it can't.
Objectively speaking, the experience and expertise required for developing buy-to-play games and those for GaaS are based on entirely different skill sets. Not only is it difficult for developers accustomed to buy-to-play games to transition to GaaS, but it’s just as challenging for those accustomed to GaaS to switch back to developing buy-to-play games. There are a lot of “you don’t know what you don’t know” issues involved.
For example, developers working under the traditional buy-to-play model often struggle to understand what players are actually consuming in games designed for long-term operation; they keep repeating that “games are supposed to be fun,” yet treat “fun” as the sole criterion for the success of GaaS.
For example, when GaaS developers switch back to creating one-time-purchase games, they are completely out of touch with the quality and polish required for the core gaming experience, as well as with an understanding of emotion, narrative, and presentation. Mr. Chen Xinghan has given so many talks in China, yet there are likely only a handful of free-to-play GaaS game developers who truly understand what he’s talking about.
These are merely issues at the design and aesthetic levels. How many GaaS developers are aware of the basic fact that “industrial pipelines are actually highly customized based on project type and cannot be reused”? And what about the delusion that a single “AAA superstar producer” can single-handedly carry a project?
These are all real-life challenges, and the gap is actually much wider than most people imagine.
However, even if the gap is huge and the challenges are immense, we still have to do it—especially for the leading tech giants, who simply must. This is because future users—or rather, current users—have already been raised on a variety of products that have set the bar high for content quality, aesthetic appeal, and service standards.
"Black Myth" has sparked a second major surge in the Chinese Steam market (the first being PUBG),As you can see, Chinese players—who are accustomed to GaaS-level services—have been extremely critical of traditional buy-to-play developers since flooding onto Steam: failing to fix optimization issues within six hours of launch is, to GaaS players, equivalent to a six-hour server crash. It’s easy to see why the negative review rate is so high.
Conversely, the same principle applies: 24 years later, players have become increasingly critical of the storytelling and aesthetics in GaaS games. Complaints about static dialogue, plot logic, and character design continue to erupt across various game communities, and this negative sentiment is spreading beyond those communities.There used to be a saying about “staying within the niche to enjoy or poke fun at ourselves,” but now, if a game is truly poorly made, bad news travels even faster. Next year, we’ll soon find out whether “mass-market aesthetics” is already a false premise (which is highly likely).
Today’s players want the quality of AAA buy-to-play content combined with top-tier studio-level GaaS operations; if that’s delivered, they’ll pay—and, as Tencent keeps emphasizing, it’s “long-term, recurring revenue.”Although *Delta* isn’t a traditional AAA buy-to-play title—it’s a PvP game—its quality alone is certainly on par with the top tier of global first-person shooters. Of course, excelling at either aspect would be enough to make it a massive hit.
So, no matter how much industry professionals and developers complain about toxic public opinion or “crazy” players, this is the challenge facing developers worldwide at this stage—it’s not something they want to learn, but something they’re forced to learn.Overseas, the shift toward Game-as-a-Service (GaaS) has entered another slump following the withdrawal of major players like Sony. The future will depend on the domestic market. While the domestic industry appears to have grasped the industrial pipeline for content creation, what it hasn’t grasped is this: both our creative pipeline and talent density fall far short of the quality standards of buy-to-play games.
Here’s a very simple example: ask any game development team in China what the day-to-day work of level designers and narrative writers actually entails.Then take a look at what these roles actually entail in development teams creating true AAA content. You’ll quickly realize just how badly we’re lacking in versatile designers who possess aesthetic sensibility, narrative expertise, and logical thinking. However, in a sense, this reflects the principle that the economic base determines the superstructure—the younger generation of designers has already demonstrated tremendous potential.
From a business perspective, this dilemma hasn’t yet become fully apparent to everyone; it’s just that people currently can’t quite envision what new possibilities exist beyond gacha games when it comes to a “one-time purchase model featuring high-quality content and a long-term gameplay experience.” And those who constantly proclaim that gacha games are dead and that SLG and card-battle games are the future—that’s far too one-sided.
This is a bit all over the place, so let me wrap it up with a conclusion: There’s a huge gap between the current state of GaaS and buy-to-play models, but the opportunities that arise from their convergence will define the next decade—opportunities that all top-tier developers will pursue. Whoever takes the initiative to truly figure out the narrative mechanics of AAA content will gain a significant head start in the next generation of content-driven GaaS products.By 2026, we’ll likely see more signs of this—perhaps.
▍Will Forest, CEO of Breaker Games
I think it’s possible to accumulate it, but it won’t make much of a difference, and you can only accumulate a very small portion of it.
According to Tencent’s definition of a long-lasting game:
"Game Tea Roundtable" is a Q&A series jointly launched by Game Tea House and Zhihu. Each week, we’ll discuss various topics with industry professionals. We also welcome you to share your thoughts in the comments section. We’ll award a Steam key for a game to the two users with the most likes in the comments section for each episode.
Mobile games with a quarterly average of more than 5 million daily active accounts, or PC games with more than 2 million, and annual revenue exceeding 4 billion yuan
Let’s break this statement down a bit—in other words, we need to do the following:
The theme appeals to a broad audience (it can attract a sufficiently large player base, ideally covering a wide range of users)
High Retention (Players who join your game and are willing to stay)
Generate Revenue (For players who stay in the game, you continuously engage them through various operational strategies and events, taking a slow and steady approach until they’re ultimately willing to spend money)
However, none of these three points are central to single-player games; let’s compare them one by one:
Broad Appeal: When it comes to single-player games, the most important thing is for the theme to be unique and explored in sufficient depth—only then can it first attract and satisfy the core player base, and only then can it break into a wider audience.
High Retention: Compared to a game's replayability or playtime, single-player games place greater emphasis on the peak experience— a game with an amazing experience can be a single-player masterpiece even if it's only 10 hours long.
Making money: That goes without saying—compared to mobile game companies, standalone game developers are practically amateurs.
Overall, developing single-player games certainly allows developers to gain experience in “how to create fun, high-quality games,” and this skill can also help with user acquisition, retention, and word-of-mouth. However, for evergreen games, this is merely the starting point of a project—not the end goal.
When a single-player game development team shifts its focus to creating evergreen games, it’s highly likely to run into many pitfalls; they’ll need to fill in the remaining 80% of their capabilities to have a chance at success. To put it more abstractly, one is building the tallest mountain, while the other is building the longest river…
▍“Traveling Thoughts” by Paranoia
Developing standalone, one-time-purchase games can provide effective content accumulation for “evergreen games” designed for long-term operation. However, they cannot provide effective accumulation for the long-term operation —particularly in terms of long-term monetization—of such “evergreen games.”
The analogy of “working through it chapter by chapter” may not be entirely appropriate. In my view, it’s unlikely that a transition from a one-time purchase model to a game-as-a-service (GaaS) model can be achieved through such incremental steps—because there are numerous chasms separating the one-time purchase model from GaaS, and working through them “chapter by chapter” will ultimately lead to a dead end.
Of course, this isn’t to say that CEO Ma is wrong, but rather that his statement is based on a certain premise: within the Tencent ecosystem, developing a long-lasting GaaS product may require “taking it one step at a time”—since Western studios lack experience with GaaS, they should give it a try;Tencent has already become highly proficient in long-term operations—particularly long-term monetization—so it now needs to gain experience in certain skills involved in single-player game development.
A buyout allows you to refine the “core fun” and productivity—such as the core gameplay and world-building: controls, camera work, enemy AI, level design, and narrative themes—which determine “why the game is worth playing long-term”;Production pipeline: resource specifications, automated builds, cross-platform submission workflows, and performance and crash management—these form the foundation for future “weekly/monthly updates”;Toolset: Level editors, numerical tables, story scripts, and batch packaging—tools that allow non-programmers to contribute directly—which directly determine long-term efficiency; Brand and user perception: IP imagery, protagonists, and aesthetics provide a “promising framework” for future seasons and events…
▍Zhihu Answerer: Yishan
Ubisoft has something to say about this. Ubisoft has been making one-time purchase games for years and has always wanted to transition to a GaaS model, but aside from *Rainbow Six: Siege* a decade ago, most of those attempts have flopped.There was a *Overwatch*-like game a while back that seems to have shut down after just a few months; *The Division 2*, a long-term service-based game, ended up with clearly insufficient endgame content in its launch version.
What is the core of GaaS? It’s about developing content once and allowing players to replay it repeatedly to reduce development costs .That’s why we see nearly all GaaS games tirelessly introducing item systems—just grind away; the more you grind, the less you hear from them. So GaaS isn’t content-driven at all, because even with today’s 42-day “sweatshop” model, players will quickly burn through the existing content.The only exception in GaaS or MMOs is the final boss of the “Icecrown Citadel” raid in *Wrath of the Lich King*, where Blizzard’s operations team actually lowered the combat difficulty to encourage players to “consume” the content as quickly as possible.but after all, this is the most iconic and arguably the most successfully developed character in the entire *Warcraft* IP—from *Warcraft* to *World of Warcraft*—bar none.
Therefore, from the planning or architectural level, GaaS requires the design of two overarching approaches—the first is how to encourage players to play repeatedly, through dungeon combinations with stats, daily, weekly, and monthly check-ins, and the design of PvP elements that let players experience the “endless fun of competing against others”;the second is to increase players’ willingness to spend—specifically, the paradigm common in domestic “gacha games,” where “stories are used to shape characters and stimulate players’ desire to pull cards” (the outfits in the *Namu Namu* series are also products of this approach, though *Namu Namu* focuses on materials and design).As for the content churn produced by sweatshop-like development, if it were all dumped on players at once, it would last no more than about 10 hours at best. The rest relies on keeping the two “overarching strategies” mentioned above in motion—the former is called DAU, and the latter is called ARPU; together, they make the whole thing work. The so-called storylines, gameplay, and content are essentially all designed to serve these principles.
But that’s not the case with full-price games. Although we acknowledge that, in the context of “Mix-Media” (media convergence), playing *Atelier* might just lead me to buy those little plastic figurines from Sega—meaning players might engage in some IP-related spending (which Kojima Studio relishes)—but when it comes down to it, the game itself is ultimately about the content.Playing *God of War: Ragnarök* on November 9, 2022, or November 9, 2025, may make no difference whatsoever in terms of the game’s essence. Santa Monica doesn’t care about your DAU—just buy it.whether you play it or not. Completion rates probably aren’t that important to Santa Monica, and even word-of-mouth isn’t that crucial (though it can serve as a basis for adjusting future content).The most important factor is clearly first-week sales—this is practically a matter of life and death for a development team. Although there are indeed titles on the market today that enjoy long-term sales success, first-week sales remain an extremely important consideration for both a studio and a publisher.
In my view, this argument is actually a form of “arrogance.” Where does this arrogance lie? It’s as if the buy-to-play model were merely a service or foundation for GaaS—as if, with development experience in buy-to-play games, studios could more easily make money off players.But unfortunately, if this narrative were truly that wonderful, Ubisoft wouldn’t be in the predicament it’s in now. Major publishers might have gone ahead and re-hired those shut-down studios, using their existing resources to create games like *Prototype Online*, *BioShock 77*, or *Canberra Hunter: Hunt the Universe*.
▍Wulang, former Tencent employee and producer of the single-player game *No One*
If the premise of this question is that “the team has already launched a long-running, evergreen game,” I think it’s feasible. First of all, in this scenario, developing a one-time purchase game likely isn’t about profit—after all, this business model can’t be compared to “in-game purchases.”It’s more likely, then, that the goal is to develop relatively low-cost “small-to-medium-sized buy-to-play games” to explore innovative gameplay or technological advancements: if a new title succeeds, these innovations can be ported to existing games to extend their lifecycles; if it fails, the cost won’t be too high.
From the perspective of player growth, if the goal is to convert players who previously didn’t play “subscription-based” games and only played “buy-to-play” games, that’s virtually impossible. In that case, it would be better to invest in a AAA title like *Black Myth*, but that’s a whole other story.
▍Producer of *Song of the Dragon: Food and Adventure*; founder of Plane Games, a studio specializing in the development of mobile games—Miyako
From mobile games to buy-to-play single-player titles, I’ve actually seen firsthand that long-term growth has real continuity. For example, with our current project, *Song of the Dragon*, we’ve already built a Discord community of over 2,000 people just during the Early Access phase. When we launch our next title, these people will be our core user base that we can reach directly.The situation is similar on Kickstarter: a core group of players who have supported us will naturally carry that support over to our next crowdfunding campaign. A prime example in the industry is the *My Time at Sandrock / My Time at Portia* series, where each installment’s crowdfunding success and community growth have surpassed that of its predecessor.While buy-to-play games don’t have “daily active users” metrics like mobile games do, they can gradually build a “long-lasting legacy” over the years through their community, reviews, and player word-of-mouth—and these accumulated assets represent tangible value for the team.
But if you’re asking whether the experience gained from the one-time purchase model can be applied to creating “evergreen” mobile games, I feel that the barrier to entry for non-one-time-purchase mobile games isn’t there—it lies in capital… Mobile games aren’t just highly competitive in terms of development; marketing and promotion costs are even higher, and it’s an oligopolistic market.
▍Jeff, a former Tencent employee and founder of the independent game studio Soda Game Studio
Speaking primarily from the perspective of small- and medium-sized/independent game studios, I’ll break the issue down into two aspects for now:
Is it feasible for small and medium-sized teams to release games on Steam—whether as one-time purchases or free-to-play titles—that are intended for long-term operation?
Is it reasonable to verify a game on the Steam Marketplace and then release a game with a similar theme and gameplay on a different platform?
I currently focus mainly on Steam games, so my perspective is somewhat limited.I know people who have developed buy-to-play games—or even free-to-play games with long-term operations—on Steam, but due to server costs, their ROI hasn’t met expectations. At least from my perspective, for small and medium-sized game developers right now, it isn’t cost-effective to release buy-to-play games with long-term operations directly on Steam during the early stages of a team’s development.
Why is that? Let’s take an example: To ensure effective operations, long-term games typically require centralized servers to store users’ in-game economic data, transaction data, and more. Steam is a global marketplace, so you need to deploy servers worldwide to guarantee a consistent experience. To save costs and handle potential traffic spikes, you also need to build a scalable server architecture and ensure server security.In addition to servers, you must also address issues such as player cheating, community management, and Steam’s stance on this type of game. These costs are quite prohibitive for most early-stage small and medium-sized teams.
Testing the gameplay through a standalone version—particularly by launching first in lightly regulated overseas markets to gather data on player engagement and other metrics—before moving on to the domestic market and mobile platforms might indeed be a good idea.A prime example is the game *Thronefall*; not only does it have its own mobile version, but other mobile games with similar gameplay are currently very popular.
But here’s a new issue: if we’re going to do it this way, I think, generally speaking, games released later need to offer higher quality, broader platform support, and more content than the games that have already been validated.I think this approach is better suited for large studios to acquire proven Steam games and re-release them across multiple platforms. For small and medium-sized game teams, setting aside whether they have the capacity for long-term operation and the necessary publishing capabilities, if you do the math, it just isn’t cost-effective. There are many ways to test the market—why choose the most expensive one?
▍Zhihu Answerer: Confused About Naming
It is possible—and there are even real-life examples.
South Korea’s “Moon Project” gained a following at Single-Player Brain Lobe, while Single-Player Ruins Library established its world-building and combat mechanics. Finally, the mobile game “Border Prison Bus” was released.
But how can I put this? In reality, doing something like this is a lot of hard work with little to show for it. For *Prison Bus* to succeed, he had to give up a lot.
First, there’s the world-building. The world of *Border Prison Bus* is so rich that you could break it down into several standalone games; without the foundation laid by the two previous installments, it would have been impossible to support such a large player base at launch.
Second, to accommodate the preferences of single-player gamers, "Border Prison" offers exceptionally generous rewards: characters come only in their base form, with no "Life Seats," no fragments, and no skill enhancements. All characters can be obtained by grinding with in-game stamina, provided you purchase the pass.
Take domestic examples of single-player games adapted into mobile games, such as *Gemland*: not only is the game world too small in the original single-player version, but the mobile version also drastically simplifies the gameplay. At the same time, the monetization model—designed to ensure revenue—is something that players of the original game simply cannot get used to.
▍Industry Observer H
A Strategy for a Student with Academic Imbalances to Turn Things Around May Not Work for Everyone
“Use single-player, full-price games to build the capabilities needed for long-term game operations.”
At first glance, this line of thinking seems sound. The Tencent team excels at “science-oriented” areas such as online game operations, monetization, and game balance design, but when it comes to “arts-oriented” areas like art, gameplay, and storytelling, they certainly can’t match the top domestic and international studios (or some of their teams).
So Tencent came up with a solution: to have students who excel in science brush up on their humanities .
This line of thinking is easy to understand. If a top student in the sciences could improve their scores in Chinese and English, wouldn’t their overall score be even higher? Tencent is that science whiz, and testing the waters with single-player, one-time-purchase games is its way of strengthening its humanities skills.By developing single-player titles, the company gains experience in art, gameplay, and storytelling—knowledge that ultimately feeds back into its own long-term, operationally-focused products.
But does this self-help plan for students who struggle in certain subjects apply to the rest of us?
The answer might be a little harsh: not really .
Why not? Take a look at these examples of failure.
The "Big Three" of the console gaming industry—Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo—have all tried their hand at service-based, long-term games. And what were the results? None of them were particularly successful.
Sony has worked the hardest and invested the most, but the results have fallen far short of expectations. As of early this year, the results of Sony’s nearly 20 GaaS projects were as follows:
Published Works:
"Hell's Commando 2," developed by Arrowhead Studios (the only successful title)
"MLB" (developed by San Diego Studio and considered a GaaS game by Sony)
"Gran Turismo 7," developed by Polyphony Digital (which Sony considers a GaaS game)
Service Termination After Launch :
"Concord," developed by Firewalk Studios (which subsequently closed)
Projects in Development :
"Marathon," developed by Bungie (expected release in 2026?)
"Fairgame$," developed by Haven Studios (scheduled for release in 2026?)
"Horizon" MMO developed by Guerrilla (release date unknown)
"Gummy Bears," developed by an unnamed studio (formerly part of Bungie; transferred to a new studio in August 2024)
An as-yet-untitled GaaS game led by Jason Blundell (former head of Deviation Games, who left the company in November 2022 and is rumored to have been recruited by Sony; several former Deviation employees are also involved in the project)
Cancelled items :
The *God of War* GaaS game developed by Bluepoint Games (development began in 2022; canceled in January 2025)
A sci-fi GaaS game developed by Bend Studio (development began around 2020; canceled in January 2025; screenshots were leaked in December 2024)
The "Twisted Metal" GaaS game developed by Firesprite (originally developed by Lucid Games, later transferred to Firesprite, and canceled in February 2024)
The *Last of Us* GaaS game developed by Naughty Dog (development began in 2020; canceled in December 2023)
The "Spider-Man" GaaS game developed by Insomniac (according to leaked information, development began in 2019 and was canceled around 2022)
An untitled GaaS game developed by Deviation Games (development began in 2021, canceled in May 2023; the studio closed in March 2024)
An untitled sci-fi GaaS game developed by First Strike Games (possibly a spin-off of the Deviation project; news of its cancellation surfaced on the same day as reports of an 80% layoff at Deviation in May 2023, though this has not yet been officially confirmed)
"Operation Payback," developed by Bungie (development reportedly began in 2022?, canceled in August 2024; believed to be "Destiny 3")
A fantasy-themed GaaS game developed by a London studio (development began in 2022, canceled in February 2024, followed by the studio's closure)
In the end, the only title Sony has left that’s worth mentioning in terms of long-term operations is *Destiny 2*, developed by the Bungie team it acquired in 2022.Bungie has become something of a “firefighter” within Sony; many of Sony’s GaaS game development teams have Bungie “supervisors” stationed on-site to guide game development, but the results have been, to put it mildly, mixed.
In fact, when judged by Chinese game developers’ standards for “long-term game operations,” *Destiny 2* is undoubtedly a “one-trick pony.”Most of *Destiny 2*’s revenue comes from large-scale DLCs released on a regular basis, which is essentially no different from other single-player, buy-to-play games that love to release DLCs (such as Paradox Interactive titles), not to mention the game’s extremely clunky onboarding and its abysmal community management.There remains a vast chasm between *Destiny 2* and true long-term operation games. And let’s not forget that the project lead for *Starfall*, widely regarded by countless players as the industry’s biggest joke of 2024, is none other than Bungie’s former CEO, Harold Ryan.
Long-running games in Europe and the U.S. simply don't buy into this approach.
In fact, it’s not that European and American developers are incapable of successfully operating long-running games. But when we look back at these successful long-running games, we find that their success often has almost nothing to do with the development teams’ experience with single-player, one-time-purchase games.
For example:
"Warframe," the renowned game from Canadian developer Digital Extremes, has been in operation for over 12 years. As another "grind-based" game, "Warframe"’s business model aligns more closely with the definition of a Game-as-a-Service (GaaS) title than that of its counterpart, "Destiny 2";
"Path of Exile," developed by the New Zealand-based studio Grinding Gear Games, released its second installment last year, and even Musk jumped on board to promote it;
as well as several multiplayer online games from Activision Blizzard, a company most people are familiar with;
And then there's Epic's *Fortnite*
The teams behind these successful long-running games from Europe and the U.S. have, for the most part, not achieved significant success with single-player, buy-to-play titles.
What does this tell us? It tells us that these two types of games are, in essence, two completely different things.
A single-player game is like making a movie, while long-term operation is like producing a TV show.
Why is it so difficult to apply the lessons learned from single-player games to games designed for long-term operation? The root cause is that these are two completely different businesses.
Developing a single-player game is like making a movie : you assemble a team of top-notch talent (a four-digit team during the “Full Production” phase), spend a huge amount of money (before the pandemic, this was roughly 60,000 to 100 million; now it basically starts at 200 million),spend 2–3 years meticulously polishing the game (now typically 3–5 years), and then pin all your hopes on the first-week or first-month box office. You’re only responsible for the 2–3 hours players spend in the theater (which corresponds to the 30–50 hours of main story content typical of single-player games).
Running a game over the long term is like producing a TV show that never goes off the air: You need to continuously produce new content, keep the audience engaged, interact with fans, and design ads and monetization opportunities so that the show can keep airing season after season.
Can a talented film director make good TV shows? Not necessarily. Conversely, can a successful TV producer make good movies? That’s also difficult.
These two types of business require completely different skill sets: single-player games prioritize the ability to create a once-in-a-lifetime experience, while long-term games require the ability to keep players coming back for more; single-player games rely on a one-time sale, whereas long-term games require a steady, sustained flow of engagement;Once a single-player game is released, the team can move on to the next project, whereas the development of a game designed for long-term operation is a never-ending process.
The financial models of the two are also completely different: for the vast majority of single-player, one-time-purchase games, more than 50% of revenue comes from the first month after release, with the remaining revenue coming from small spikes generated by subsequent sales and promotions.In the early stages of long-term game operations, many titles operate at a loss to build a following; they require continuous efforts to maintain engagement and positive word-of-mouth in order to secure a stable, steady stream of revenue over the long term.
So, can single-player games really help build the capabilities needed for long-term game operations?
The answer is: It depends on the person .
For a “tech-focused powerhouse” like Tencent, which has two decades of experience operating online games, developing single-player games could indeed help address its weaknesses in art and storytelling.
But for most teams, blindly jumping on the bandwagon to develop single-player games is likely just a waste of resources, and they’ll end up with a set of skills they can’t put to use.
The biggest pitfall in the gaming industry is treating “quick fixes” as “panaceas.” No matter how well a single-player game is made, it doesn’t necessarily guarantee long-term success. Every game genre has its own rules, and true success comes from respecting and understanding the unique characteristics of each format—not from simply assuming that one set of experiences can be directly replicated in another.

In today's gaming industry, it's becoming increasingly difficult to achieve overnight success.

Recently, Ma Xiaoyi, Senior Vice President of Tencent, mentioned in an interview that creating a long-lasting GaaS product might require “taking it one chapter at a time”—with long-term operation as the ultimate goal, the team might be able to gradually build and validate its capabilities in gameplay, storytelling, and other areas by developing single-player, one-time-purchase titles.

In terms of business models, service-based games offer far greater revenue sustainability and potential than single-player buy-to-play titles. But just as a carp leaps through the Dragon Gate, behind every successful, long-running game there may be countless competitors that have fallen by the wayside—and no one dares to claim with absolute certainty that they have mastered all the necessary conditions for success.Even Ma Xiaoyi admits that a game may need to meet 10 prerequisites just to qualify for the “lottery,” and even then, the odds of winning may be as low as 30 percent.

Developing evergreen games is challenging. If you have to consider long-term operations while refining gameplay and storytelling, the complexity increases exponentially. That’s why Tencent is open to breaking this process down internally and iterating over several generations, and it also supports teams exploring new approaches through single-player, one-time-purchase games.

This process is undoubtedly challenging: Developing a single-player game is relatively straightforward, but long-term operation, monetization, multiplayer online gameplay, social competition, cross-platform support… every keyword associated with creating a long-lasting game seems like an insurmountable barrier. Can the gap between buy-to-play and subscription-based games truly be bridged through accumulated experience?

In this episode of “Game & Tea Roundtable,” we spoke with industry professionals about whether developing single-player, buy-out games can truly contribute to the long-term growth of “evergreen games” designed for sustained operation.

▍Industry Troll: Xiao Jiu

It can, but it can't.

Objectively speaking, the experience and expertise required for developing buy-to-play games and those for GaaS are based on entirely different skill sets. Not only is it difficult for developers accustomed to buy-to-play games to transition to GaaS, but it’s just as challenging for those accustomed to GaaS to switch back to developing buy-to-play games. There are a lot of “you don’t know what you don’t know” issues involved.

For example, developers working under the traditional buy-to-play model often struggle to understand what players are actually consuming in games designed for long-term operation; they keep repeating that “games are supposed to be fun,” yet treat “fun” as the sole criterion for the success of GaaS.

For example, when GaaS developers switch back to creating one-time-purchase games, they are completely out of touch with the quality and polish required for the core gaming experience, as well as with an understanding of emotion, narrative, and presentation. Mr. Chen Xinghan has given so many talks in China, yet there are likely only a handful of free-to-play GaaS game developers who truly understand what he’s talking about.

These are merely issues at the design and aesthetic levels. How many GaaS developers are aware of the basic fact that “industrial pipelines are actually highly customized based on project type and cannot be reused”? And what about the delusion that a single “AAA superstar producer” can single-handedly carry a project?

These are all real-life challenges, and the gap is actually much wider than most people imagine.

However, even if the gap is huge and the challenges are immense, we still have to do it—especially for the leading tech giants, who simply must. This is because future users—or rather, current users—have already been raised on a variety of products that have set the bar high for content quality, aesthetic appeal, and service standards.

"Black Myth" has sparked a second major surge in the Chinese Steam market (the first being PUBG),As you can see, Chinese players—who are accustomed to GaaS-level services—have been extremely critical of traditional buy-to-play developers since flooding onto Steam: failing to fix optimization issues within six hours of launch is, to GaaS players, equivalent to a six-hour server crash. It’s easy to see why the negative review rate is so high.

Conversely, the same principle applies: 24 years later, players have become increasingly critical of the storytelling and aesthetics in GaaS games. Complaints about static dialogue, plot logic, and character design continue to erupt across various game communities, and this negative sentiment is spreading beyond those communities.There used to be a saying about “staying within the niche to enjoy or poke fun at ourselves,” but now, if a game is truly poorly made, bad news travels even faster. Next year, we’ll soon find out whether “mass-market aesthetics” is already a false premise (which is highly likely).

Today’s players want the quality of AAA buy-to-play content combined with top-tier studio-level GaaS operations; if that’s delivered, they’ll pay—and, as Tencent keeps emphasizing, it’s “long-term, recurring revenue.”Although *Delta* isn’t a traditional AAA buy-to-play title—it’s a PvP game—its quality alone is certainly on par with the top tier of global first-person shooters. Of course, excelling at either aspect would be enough to make it a massive hit.

So, no matter how much industry professionals and developers complain about toxic public opinion or “crazy” players, this is the challenge facing developers worldwide at this stage—it’s not something they want to learn, but something they’re forced to learn.Overseas, the shift toward Game-as-a-Service (GaaS) has entered another slump following the withdrawal of major players like Sony. The future will depend on the domestic market. While the domestic industry appears to have grasped the industrial pipeline for content creation, what it hasn’t grasped is this: both our creative pipeline and talent density fall far short of the quality standards of buy-to-play games.

Here’s a very simple example: ask any game development team in China what the day-to-day work of level designers and narrative writers actually entails.Then take a look at what these roles actually entail in development teams creating true AAA content. You’ll quickly realize just how badly we’re lacking in versatile designers who possess aesthetic sensibility, narrative expertise, and logical thinking. However, in a sense, this reflects the principle that the economic base determines the superstructure—the younger generation of designers has already demonstrated tremendous potential.

From a business perspective, this dilemma hasn’t yet become fully apparent to everyone; it’s just that people currently can’t quite envision what new possibilities exist beyond gacha games when it comes to a “one-time purchase model featuring high-quality content and a long-term gameplay experience.” And those who constantly proclaim that gacha games are dead and that SLG and card-battle games are the future—that’s far too one-sided.

This is a bit all over the place, so let me wrap it up with a conclusion: There’s a huge gap between the current state of GaaS and buy-to-play models, but the opportunities that arise from their convergence will define the next decade—opportunities that all top-tier developers will pursue. Whoever takes the initiative to truly figure out the narrative mechanics of AAA content will gain a significant head start in the next generation of content-driven GaaS products.By 2026, we’ll likely see more signs of this—perhaps.

▍Will Forest, CEO of Breaker Games

I think it’s possible to accumulate it, but it won’t make much of a difference, and you can only accumulate a very small portion of it.

According to Tencent’s definition of a long-lasting game:

Let’s break this statement down a bit—in other words, we need to do the following:

  • The theme appeals to a broad audience (it can attract a sufficiently large player base, ideally covering a wide range of users)
  • High Retention (Players who join your game and are willing to stay)
  • Generate Revenue (For players who stay in the game, you continuously engage them through various operational strategies and events, taking a slow and steady approach until they’re ultimately willing to spend money)

However, none of these three points are central to single-player games; let’s compare them one by one:

Broad Appeal: When it comes to single-player games, the most important thing is for the theme to be unique and explored in sufficient depth—only then can it first attract and satisfy the core player base, and only then can it break into a wider audience.

High Retention: Compared to a game's replayability or playtime, single-player games place greater emphasis on the peak experience—a game with an amazing experience can be a single-player masterpiece even if it's only 10 hours long.

Making money: That goes without saying—compared to mobile game companies, standalone game developers are practically amateurs.

Overall, developing single-player games certainly allows developers to gain experience in “how to create fun, high-quality games,” and this skill can also help with user acquisition, retention, and word-of-mouth. However, for evergreen games, this is merely the starting point of a project—not the end goal.

When a single-player game development team shifts its focus to creating evergreen games, it’s highly likely to run into many pitfalls; they’ll need to fill in the remaining 80% of their capabilities to have a chance at success. To put it more abstractly, one is building the tallest mountain, while the other is building the longest river…

▍“Traveling Thoughts” by Paranoia

Developing standalone, one-time-purchase games can provide effective content accumulation for “evergreen games” designed for long-term operation. However, they cannot provide effective accumulation for the long-term operation—particularly in terms of long-term monetization—of such “evergreen games.”

The analogy of “working through it chapter by chapter” may not be entirely appropriate. In my view, it’s unlikely that a transition from a one-time purchase model to a game-as-a-service (GaaS) model can be achieved through such incremental steps—because there are numerous chasms separating the one-time purchase model from GaaS, and working through them “chapter by chapter” will ultimately lead to a dead end.

Of course, this isn’t to say that CEO Ma is wrong, but rather that his statement is based on a certain premise: within the Tencent ecosystem, developing a long-lasting GaaS product may require “taking it one step at a time”—since Western studios lack experience with GaaS, they should give it a try;Tencent has already become highly proficient in long-term operations—particularly long-term monetization—so it now needs to gain experience in certain skills involved in single-player game development.

A buyout allows you to refine the “core fun” and productivity—such as the core gameplay and world-building: controls, camera work, enemy AI, level design, and narrative themes—which determine “why the game is worth playing long-term”;Production pipeline: resource specifications, automated builds, cross-platform submission workflows, and performance and crash management—these form the foundation for future “weekly/monthly updates”;Toolset: Level editors, numerical tables, story scripts, and batch packaging—tools that allow non-programmers to contribute directly—which directly determine long-term efficiency; Brand and user perception: IP imagery, protagonists, and aesthetics provide a “promising framework” for future seasons and events…

▍Zhihu Answerer: Yishan

Ubisoft has something to say about this. Ubisoft has been making one-time purchase games for years and has always wanted to transition to a GaaS model, but aside from *Rainbow Six: Siege* a decade ago, most of those attempts have flopped.There was a *Overwatch*-like game a while back that seems to have shut down after just a few months; *The Division 2*, a long-term service-based game, ended up with clearly insufficient endgame content in its launch version.

What is the core of GaaS? It’s about developing content once and allowing players to replay it repeatedly to reduce development costs.That’s why we see nearly all GaaS games tirelessly introducing item systems—just grind away; the more you grind, the less you hear from them. So GaaS isn’t content-driven at all, because even with today’s 42-day “sweatshop” model, players will quickly burn through the existing content.The only exception in GaaS or MMOs is the final boss of the “Icecrown Citadel” raid in *Wrath of the Lich King*, where Blizzard’s operations team actually lowered the combat difficulty to encourage players to “consume” the content as quickly as possible.but after all, this is the most iconic and arguably the most successfully developed character in the entire *Warcraft* IP—from *Warcraft* to *World of Warcraft*—bar none.

Therefore, from the planning or architectural level, GaaS requires the design of two overarching approaches—the first is how to encourage players to play repeatedly, through dungeon combinations with stats, daily, weekly, and monthly check-ins, and the design of PvP elements that let players experience the “endless fun of competing against others”;the second is to increase players’ willingness to spend—specifically, the paradigm common in domestic “gacha games,” where “stories are used to shape characters and stimulate players’ desire to pull cards” (the outfits in the *Namu Namu* series are also products of this approach, though *Namu Namu* focuses on materials and design).As for the content churn produced by sweatshop-like development, if it were all dumped on players at once, it would last no more than about 10 hours at best. The rest relies on keeping the two “overarching strategies” mentioned above in motion—the former is called DAU, and the latter is called ARPU; together, they make the whole thing work. The so-called storylines, gameplay, and content are essentially all designed to serve these principles.

But that’s not the case with full-price games. Although we acknowledge that, in the context of “Mix-Media” (media convergence), playing *Atelier* might just lead me to buy those little plastic figurines from Sega—meaning players might engage in some IP-related spending (which Kojima Studio relishes)—but when it comes down to it, the game itself is ultimately about the content.Playing *God of War: Ragnarök* on November 9, 2022, or November 9, 2025, may make no difference whatsoever in terms of the game’s essence. Santa Monica doesn’t care about your DAU—just buy it.whether you play it or not. Completion rates probably aren’t that important to Santa Monica, and even word-of-mouth isn’t that crucial (though it can serve as a basis for adjusting future content).The most important factor is clearly first-week sales—this is practically a matter of life and death for a development team. Although there are indeed titles on the market today that enjoy long-term sales success, first-week sales remain an extremely important consideration for both a studio and a publisher.

In my view, this argument is actually a form of “arrogance.” Where does this arrogance lie? It’s as if the buy-to-play model were merely a service or foundation for GaaS—as if, with development experience in buy-to-play games, studios could more easily make money off players.But unfortunately, if this narrative were truly that wonderful, Ubisoft wouldn’t be in the predicament it’s in now. Major publishers might have gone ahead and re-hired those shut-down studios, using their existing resources to create games like *Prototype Online*, *BioShock 77*, or *Canberra Hunter: Hunt the Universe*.

▍Wulang, former Tencent employee and producer of the single-player game *No One*

If the premise of this question is that “the team has already launched a long-running, evergreen game,” I think it’s feasible. First of all, in this scenario, developing a one-time purchase game likely isn’t about profit—after all, this business model can’t be compared to “in-game purchases.”It’s more likely, then, that the goal is to develop relatively low-cost “small-to-medium-sized buy-to-play games” to explore innovative gameplay or technological advancements: if a new title succeeds, these innovations can be ported to existing games to extend their lifecycles; if it fails, the cost won’t be too high.

From the perspective of player growth, if the goal is to convert players who previously didn’t play “subscription-based” games and only played “buy-to-play” games, that’s virtually impossible. In that case, it would be better to invest in a AAA title like *Black Myth*, but that’s a whole other story.

▍Producer of *Song of the Dragon: Food and Adventure*; founder of Plane Games, a studio specializing in the development of mobile games—Miyako

From mobile games to buy-to-play single-player titles, I’ve actually seen firsthand that long-term growth has real continuity. For example, with our current project, *Song of the Dragon*, we’ve already built a Discord community of over 2,000 people just during the Early Access phase. When we launch our next title, these people will be our core user base that we can reach directly.The situation is similar on Kickstarter: a core group of players who have supported us will naturally carry that support over to our next crowdfunding campaign.
